Safe-harbour prongs are disjunctive (meaningful cautionary language OR no actual knowledge), so the CEO's actual knowledge does not defeat the cautionary-language prong; choice 3's 'unless made with actual knowledge' merges the prongs imprecisely but is still the best answer.

claims.claim: Apparent authority rests on the principal's manifestations to the third party that lead the third party reasonably to believe the agent is authorised.
Agency arises from the principal's manifestation of assent that the agent act on its behalf and subject to its control, with the agent's consent; no contract or consideration needed.
claims.note: Matches Restatement (Third) 1.01 from memory; the Wex agency page opened does not state the control element.

claims.claim: Ratification requires knowledge of material facts and must cover the whole transaction; it relates back to the time of the act.
claims.note: Consistent with Restatement (Third) 4.02, 4.06, 4.07 from memory; Wex ratification page returned no usable text.

claims.claim: Respondeat superior makes an employer liable for employee torts within the scope of employment.
A minor deviation (detour) remains within scope; a substantial personal errand (frolic) usually falls outside.
A partially disclosed principal is bound and the agent is also a party to the contract.
claims.note: Matches Restatement (Third) 6.02 from memory; no page opened.

claims.claim: Sharing profits gives rise to an inference of partnership, except when received as wages, rent, interest on a loan, or for goodwill.
claims.note: Checked against Delaware's RUPA-based 6 Del. C. 15-202(c)(3), which says 'presumed'; RUPA 1997 also says 'presumed', so 'prima facie evidence' is UPA 1914 phrasing but substantively close.

claims.claim: All partners are jointly and severally liable; a newly admitted partner is not personally liable for obligations incurred before admission.
A person who holds himself out as a partner and induces reliance can be liable as a partner by estoppel.
The 2001 Uniform Limited Partnership Act abandoned the control rule for limited partners.
Delaware's LLC Act permits the operating agreement to expand, restrict or eliminate fiduciary duties but not the implied contractual covenant of good faith and fair dealing.
Most states' LLP statutes now shield partners from contract as well as tort obligations; early statutes covered only tort.
claims.note: A minority of states still give only a partial shield.

claims.claim: S corporations are limited to 100 shareholders, may not have nonresident alien shareholders, and may have only one class of stock.
CTS Corp. v. Dynamics Corp. of America (1987) upheld Indiana's control-share statute and described the internal affairs doctrine as ensuring only one state governs a corporation's internal affairs.
Delaware's 2025 SB 21: 'the effects and constitutionality of those changes continue to be litigated and debated.'
claims.note: Stale: on Feb 27, 2026 the Delaware Supreme Court (en banc) in Rutledge v. Clearway Energy Group LLC upheld the constitutionality of SB 21's DGCL 144 amendments.

claims.claim: A de facto corporation requires a statute permitting incorporation, a good-faith attempt to comply, and actual use of corporate privileges.
In Delaware, preemptive rights exist only if the charter grants them.
Under MBCA section 2.04, persons acting on behalf of a corporation knowing none has been formed are jointly and severally liable.
claims.note: Matches MBCA 2.04 from memory; no page with the MBCA text was opened.

claims.claim: United States v. Bestfoods (1998): a parent is liable under CERCLA if the veil is pierced or the parent directly operated the facility, not merely because it is a parent.
Walkovszky v. Carlton was a New York case decided in 1966.
'Courts are more willing to pierce in contract cases where a creditor was misled ... than in tort cases'; empirical work, 'however', shows piercing succeeds more often in contract cases.
claims.note: Paragraph is internally muddled: the conventional doctrinal view is that courts say they are MORE willing to pierce for involuntary tort creditors, while Thompson's empirical study found more piercing in contract cases; the 'however' contrast is inverted. Not checked against an opened source.

claims.claim: Delaware permits dividends out of surplus, or if none, out of net profits for the current and/or preceding fiscal year.
claims.note: 8 Del. C. 170(a); director liability under 174 with subrogation against knowing recipients.

claims.claim: A sale of all or substantially all assets requires board action then approval by a majority of the outstanding voting stock in Delaware.
Dodge v. Ford Motor Co. was decided by the Michigan Supreme Court in 1919 and is cited for shareholder primacy.
Smith v. Van Gorkom (Del. 1985) held Trans Union directors grossly negligent and prompted adoption of DGCL 102(b)(7).
In re Walt Disney Co. Derivative Litigation (Del. 2006) found the directors not liable.
Under DGCL 141(e), directors are fully protected in relying in good faith on reports of officers, committees and experts selected with reasonable care.

Modern statutes such as DGCL 144 say a conflicted transaction is not void or voidable solely because of the interest if it passes a cleansing mechanism (disinterested directors, shareholders, or fairness).
claims.note: Describes pre-2025 text. Current 8 Del. C. 144(a) (as amended by SB 21, 2025) says a compliant transaction 'may not be the subject of equitable relief, or give rise to an award of damages'; stockholder approval is a majority of votes cast by disinterested stockholders; if a majority of the board is not disinterested, a committee of 2+ disinterested directors must approve; separate controller safe harbors in 144(b)-(c).

claims.claim: Benihana of Tokyo, Inc. v. Benihana, Inc. was decided by the Delaware Supreme Court in 2005.
claims.note: Delaware Supreme Court decision is 906 A.2d 114 (Del. 2006); the Chancery decision was 2005. Holding as described is correct.

claims.claim: SB 21's validity challenges 'are being worked out' and Delaware law is in transition.
claims.note: Delaware Supreme Court upheld SB 21's 144 amendments in Rutledge v. Clearway Energy Group LLC (Feb 27, 2026).

claims.claim: Guth v. Loft, Inc. (Del. 1939) and Broz v. Cellular Information Systems (Del. 1996) set Delaware's corporate opportunity test.
DGCL 122(17) lets a corporation renounce in its charter any expectancy in specified business opportunities.
claims.note: Also permits renunciation by board action.

claims.claim: Kahn v. M&F Worldwide (Del. 2014) gives business judgment review to controller buyouts conditioned ab initio on special committee and majority-of-minority approval; Weinberger v. UOP (Del. 1983).
claims.note: 88 A.3d 635 (Del. 2014); 457 A.2d 701 (Del. 1983). Note SB 21 (2025) now provides statutory controller safe harbors in DGCL 144(b)-(c) (non-going-private deals can be cleansed by committee OR disinterested-stockholder vote), upheld in Rutledge v. Clearway (Del. Feb 27, 2026); the lesson flags the change but not that it survived challenge.

claims.claim: Caremark (Del. Ch. 1996), Stone v. Ritter (Del. 2006) and Marchand v. Barnhill (Del. 2019) define oversight liability.
DGCL 102(b)(7) now extends exculpation to officers, but not in actions by or in the right of the corporation.
Under DGCL 145(c), a director or officer successful on the merits or otherwise must be indemnified for expenses; 145(b) limits indemnification in derivative suits.
In Delaware, cumulative voting exists only if the charter provides for it; directors are elected by plurality by default.
Schnell v. Chris-Craft Industries (Del. 1971): inequitable action does not become permissible simply because it is legally possible.
Delaware amended section 220 in 2025 to define inspectable books and records more narrowly.
claims.note: Current 220 lists specific records (e.g., minutes and consents for 3 years) and limits what Chancery may order beyond them.

claims.claim: Zapata Corp. v. Maldonado (Del. 1981) set the two-step review of special litigation committee dismissal motions.
Auerbach v. Bennett (N.Y. 1979) adopted a more deferential SLC review.
United Food & Commercial Workers Union v. Zuckerberg (Del. 2021) consolidated Aronson and Rales into a director-by-director test; demand futile if at least half the board fails.

claims.claim: Donahue v. Rodd Electrotype (Mass. 1975) and Wilkes v. Springside Nursing Home (Mass. 1976) set Massachusetts close-corporation fiduciary rules (legitimate business purpose / less harmful alternative).
Nixon v. Blackwell (Del. 1993) declined special judicial rules for non-statutory close corporations; McQuade v. Stoneham (N.Y. 1934), Clark v. Dodge (N.Y. 1936).
MBCA section 14.30 permits dissolution for illegal, fraudulent or oppressive conduct toward the complaining shareholder.

claims.claim: A short-form merger is available when a parent owns at least 90 percent of a subsidiary, with no minority vote (DGCL 253).
DGCL 262 appraisal has a market-out exception for listed/widely held shares receiving listed stock, with exceptions where cash is paid.
Farris v. Glen Alden (Pa. 1958) adopted de facto merger; Hariton v. Arco Electronics (Del. 1963) adopted independent legal significance.
claims.note: Hariton Chancery opinion is 1962; Delaware Supreme Court affirmed in 1963.

claims.claim: DGCL 203 bars business combinations with a 15 percent holder for three years unless conditions are met.
Unocal (Del. 1985), Moran v. Household (Del. 1985), Revlon (Del. 1986), Unitrin (Del. 1995), Omnicare (Del. 2003), Corwin (Del. 2015).
Paramount Communications v. QVC Network (Del. 1994) triggered Revlon on a sale of control.
claims.note: Consistent with my knowledge (637 A.2d 34 (Del. 1994)); no page opened.

claims.claim: Accredited investor natural-person thresholds: $200,000 income ($300,000 joint) or net worth over $1 million excluding primary residence.
Rule 506(b) allows up to 35 non-accredited purchasers without general solicitation; 506(c) requires reasonable steps to verify accredited status.
Howey (1946), Ralston Purina (1953) and Gustafson v. Alloyd (1995) as described.
Ernst & Ernst v. Hochfelder (1976) requires scienter; Blue Chip Stamps (1975) limits private suits to purchasers and sellers.
Basic Inc. v. Levinson (1988) adopted the fraud-on-the-market presumption and probability/magnitude materiality for merger talks.
Morrison v. National Australia Bank (2010) limits 10(b) to securities listed on domestic exchanges and domestic transactions.

The SEC amended Rule 10b5-1 in 2022 to add cooling-off periods, good-faith conditions and disclosure requirements.
Civil penalty for insider trading up to three times the profit gained or loss avoided.
